1:
"These things have I spoken unto you, that ye should not be offended." The witnesses read Christ's purpose in forewarning the disciples of coming persecution — to fortify them against stumbling when the hatred of the world breaks out.

The Latin and Eastern fathers read the strengthening aim. Augustine: after the promise of the Spirit "to inspire them with strength to give witness," he adds this "that you should not be offended," for "when the love of God is shed" abroad the soul stands firm. Chrysostom recalls that the Jews had already agreed to expel any who confessed Christ (John 9:22). Augustine of Hippo notes he had "prepared them by his own example to become the more courageous."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the word. Barnes: "offend" here means "to stumble or fall — that is, to apostatize" (Matthew 5:29). Robertson: the purpose clause with "made to stumble" (skandalisthēte), "the stumblingblocks which trip up a disciple" (1 John 2:10). Ellicott refers it to "the things which he had just said" of the world's hatred and the Spirit's witness (John 15:18-27).

The Reformed and Puritan voices read the pastoral prudence. Calvin: "none of these warnings are superfluous; for, since wars and contests await them, it is necessary that they should be provided beforehand with the necessary arms" — and what he said to the disciples "is also spoken to us." Henry: "Christ dealt faithfully with his disciples... he told them the worst of it, that they might sit down and count the cost." The upshot is plain: forewarning is itself a weapon — Christ arms his own against offence by telling them plainly what is to come, that the shock of persecution may not shake their faith (v.4).

Augustine supplies the reason the forewarning works at all. When "the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit which is given to us" (Romans 5:5), then great peace belongs to those who love his law, and they are not offended at it. The promise of the Spirit stands first, and the warning follows it, because only the strength of the one can carry a man through the other.

Calvin's word holds: what was spoken to the eleven is spoken also to the church in every age that faces the same hatred (John 15:18).
2:
The double cost of discipleship — excommunication and martyrdom, the latter committed in the name of religion — is what the saying lays bare: "They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the terms. Robertson: "they will make you outcasts from the synagogues" (aposynagōgous, 9:22; 12:42). Ellicott: "will think that he offereth to God a sacrificial service" — the word "is the technical word for offering sacrifice," so murder is mistaken for worship. Barnes lists the persecutions to come (Acts 9:1-2; cf. Acts 26:9). Lightfoot notes the casting out was "from the whole congregation of Israel," as with the Samaritans.

The Reformed voice reads the trial to the conscience. Calvin: "it was no light offence... that they were to be banished like wicked men from the assembly of the godly," for believers face "not only persecutions, but ignominy and reproaches" (1 Corinthians 4:12-13). Gill recalls the law already made against confessors and its terror upon the people.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke notes that excommunication stripped them of substance and civil fellowship (Ezra 10:8; Hebrews 10:34). Wesley draws a grateful contrast: "blessed be God, the time is so far past, that those who bear the name of Christ do not now generally suppose they do him service by killing each other for a difference in opinion." One conclusion is pressed from every side: the deepest peril is not open hatred but persecution dressed as piety — men killing the saints and calling it sacrifice to God; the very horror Christ traces, in the next verse, to ignorance of the Father and the Son (v.3).

Gill measures the sentence precisely, and it is heavier than the English suggests. The expulsion meant is not the lesser censure, the Niddui, which parted a man from one synagogue for a season, but the greater, by Cherem or Shammatha, which cut him off from the whole body of the nation. He recalls that the law had already been made and already enforced, upon the blind man who confessed his healer, and that the fear of it kept even believing rulers silent, since to be reckoned a heretic and apostate was more than they could bear.

Paul, who once thus 'verily thought' he ought to oppose the Name (Acts 26:9), became the standing proof that such sincerity is no innocence.
3:
The root of all religious persecution — ignorance of God as he is revealed in Christ — is what this verse names: "And these things will they do unto you, because they have not known the Father, nor me."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the cause. Robertson: "definite reason for the religious hatred is ignorance of God and Christ" (John 15:21). Ellicott: "ignorance of God revealed in himself" — there is "a special force" in this, for "men think that in exclusion" of the saints they serve God, while in truth they know neither Father nor Son (1 Corinthians 2:8; 1 Timothy 1:13).

The Reformed voice draws the comfort and the warning. Calvin: "not without good reason does Christ frequently remind the apostles" that "there is only one reason why unbelievers are so greatly enraged against them — it is because they do not know God"; this is said "not to extenuate their guilt, but that the apostles may boldly despise their blind fury." Gill: it was "pure wilful ignorance of the Father and himself."

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke states it as a maxim: "ignorance of the benevolence of God, and of the philanthropy of Christ, is the grand fountain whence all religious persecution and intolerance proceed." Wesley: "this is the true root of persecution in all its forms." All four trace it to a single root: the persecutors' zeal, however sincere, springs from a fatal ignorance — they do not know the God they think they serve, for they have rejected the Son in whom alone the Father is known (v.2); and Christ tells his own this beforehand, the next verse adds, that the event may confirm rather than shake their faith (v.4).

Ellicott binds the verse tightly to the one before it, and the force of the link is worth feeling. Men suppose that in exclusions and anathemas, in the killing of others made like themselves in the image of God, they offer an acceptable sacrifice; and they can know nothing of "the true nature of the living Father who pitieth every child, and willeth not the death of a sinner." The ignorance is not of God in general but of God revealed in the Son.

To know God in Christ, the chapter implies, is the only cure for the spirit that persecutes (John 17:3).
4:
Christ's reason for the forewarning — that the fulfilment, when it comes, will strengthen rather than shatter faith — comes into view at once: "But these things have I told you, that when the time shall come, ye may remember that I told you of them."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the aim. Barnes: "by calling to mind that he had foretold these things they would perceive that he was omniscient," and remember "the consolations" he had given. Robertson: the perfect "have I spoken" (a solemn repetition), with the indefinite "whenever their hour comes." Ellicott: "he strengthens them by forewarning" (John 13:19; John 14:29) — "when the persecution comes they will... find in it support for their faith and evidence of his presence."

The Eastern father reads the timing tenderly. Chrysostom: "great is the tyranny of despondency," and Christ gauges what they can bear; Clarke gives Christ's own reason — "I would not trouble you by speaking pointedly at first... lest you should be discouraged," but now declares it "because it is absolutely necessary that you should be put upon your guard." Wesley: "I did not tell you these things at the beginning, because I was with you — to bear the chief shock in my own person, and to screen you from it."

The Reformed voice reads the practical end. Calvin: "this is not a philosophy fitted only for a season of leisure, but adapted to practice and use"; he discourses on these matters "that they may actually demonstrate that they have not been taught in vain," laying up his words in their minds against the day of need. The purpose of the warning is thus clear: Christ forewarns not to alarm but to fortify — withholding the full weight of it while he was present to shield them, and now arming them, so that the very arrival of persecution would become a proof of his foreknowledge and a comfort in their grief, which he turns to address next (v.5).

He had spared them the full weight while he was with them to bear the shock; now, as he goes, he arms them — and turns to address the grief his going has stirred (v.5).
5:
"But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?" The witnesses read Christ's gentle reproof — the disciples, drowned in grief, fail to ask where he is going.

The Eastern and Latin fathers read the correction. Chrysostom: "the disciples, not as yet perfected, being overcome by sorrow, our Lord blames and corrects them." Augustine notes the contrast that the Spirit, poured into the disciples "throughout the whole world," would reprove not one nation only.

The grammatical-historical readers reconcile the apparent puzzle. Clarke: Peter (John 13:36) and Thomas (John 14:5) had earlier asked "whither goest thou?" and been answered, "but now" none asks, "because their hearts were filled with sorrow" (v.6). Robertson: "now that they realize Jesus is going, the thoughts of the disciples turn on themselves and they cease asking." Barnes: "had they made the inquiry, he was ready to answer and to comfort them."

The Reformed voice reads the consolation behind the rebuke. Calvin: "by a very excellent consolation he assuages the grief which they might feel on account of his departure"; what would have become of them, called now "to severe and arduous battles," "if they had not known that Christ was in heaven, as the guardian" of their salvation. Wesley: none asks "now when it is most seasonable." What the reproof amounts to is this: the reproof is tender — Christ would have them lift their eyes from their own loss to his going to the Father, which is the very ground of their comfort and the condition of the Spirit's coming (v.7).

Their failure to ask 'whither?' is the measure of a grief too self-absorbed to see the glory toward which he goes (v.6).

Augustine offers a second way of taking the complaint. Earlier they had asked where he was going, and had been told he went where they could not follow; now he promises to go in such a manner that none of them will ask it again. On that reading the silence is not merely their failure but the shape of what he is doing, a departure that will answer the question instead of leaving it open.

Their silence, and that, as the commentators mark, was not contentment but a grief that had eclipsed the very Lord who was its object (v.6).
6:
The disciples' grief — so absorbing that it crowds out both inquiry and comfort — is all the verse records: "But because I have said these things unto you, sorrow hath filled your heart."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the note. Robertson: "sorrow hath filled" (perfect active) — "they do not see their way to go on without Jesus"; the word for sorrow is used of them only in this chapter. Ellicott: "the thought of their own separation from him, and of the dark future... so filled their hearts that it left room for no thoughts of him, and the brightness of the glory to which he was returning."

Gill lists the causes of the sorrow — the hatred and persecution foretold, being put out of the synagogues, the loss of life, and "particularly" the loss of Christ's bodily presence. The grief is real and not rebuked as sin, but as a thing to be lifted above.

The Eastern Chrysostom presses the same point and finds comfort in it, marking how wholly they were struck down: hearing that their killers would think they did God service, they could say nothing at all; yet it was "no small consolation to them to know that the Lord knew their superabundant sorrow," both for his leaving them and for the evils they were told to expect, not knowing whether they would suffer manfully. The Latin Augustine traces the cause deeper. Lacking as yet "that inward consolation which the Holy Ghost was to impart," they were afraid to lose the outward presence of Christ; and when his own words left them no room for doubt, "their human affections were saddened, for the loss of their visible object." Yet he knew their loss would be their gain, since the inward sight the Spirit would give them was the better one.

The diagnosis is agreed: the verse diagnoses the disciples' state — a sorrow so total that it had become self-absorbed, fixed on their own loss rather than on the Lord's gain in returning to the Father. It is the very condition Christ now begins to heal, turning their eyes from his departure to its benefit, for it is precisely his going that will bring the Comforter (v.7). The grief that filled their hearts (cf. v.22) will, he promises, be turned into a joy no man can take away.
7:
The great paradox — Christ's departure is gain, for it brings the Spirit — is the hard word here: "It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you; but if I depart, I will send him unto you."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the claim. Robertson: sympherei hymin, "it is expedient for you" (the same phrase as Caiaphas's in John 11:50, but "for you"). Ellicott notes the emphatic "I, who know all," prefacing words "of strange sound for the ears of disciples." Barnes asks why the Spirit's presence is "more valuable than that of the Saviour himself," answering that by his departure Christ would make atonement, ascend, and send the Spirit to be everywhere present with all believers at once.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke reads the divine order: "by the order of God, the Holy Spirit cannot come... unless he first die" — the necessity of his death (Matthew 20:19) here implied. The Puritan Henry: as the prophets comforted the church with the promise of Messiah, "the Messiah being come," he comforts with the promise of the Spirit.

The Reformed voice reads the weaning. Calvin: Christ "testifies that his absence will be advantageous," making "a sort of oath," because "we are carnal, and nothing is more difficult than to tear from our minds this foolish inclination, by which we attempt to draw down Christ from heaven to us." Wesley sums the chapter's structure: it is expedient "in respect of the Comforter, and of me, and of the Father." The conclusion runs clean against instinct: against every instinct, the bodily departure of Christ is the disciples' gain — for only so comes the Spirit, who will make Christ present to them and in them more intimately than his flesh ever could; and the Spirit's first work, the next verses unfold, will be to convict the world (v.8).

Calvin's image holds — we must be weaned from drawing Christ down to us, and learn to seek him where he is, that the Spirit's work may begin (v.8).
8:
"And when he is come, he will reprove the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment." The witnesses read the Spirit's threefold work upon the world — and prefer "convince" or "convict" to "reprove."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the verb. Barnes: "reprove" means "to demonstrate by argument, to prove, to convince... and particularly to convince of crime" — "he will convince or convict the world of sin." Robertson: elegxei, "convicting by proof" (John 3:20; John 8:46); Jesus had begun this (John 7:7), but the Spirit will carry it on. Ellicott prefers "convince the world," the only Gospel parallels being Matthew 18:15 and Luke 3:19.

The Latin and Wesleyan-Arminian voices read the scope. Augustine of Hippo opens the question of what the threefold conviction means. Clarke: the Spirit "will demonstrate these matters so clearly as to leave no doubt," first to "the Jewish nation" (Acts 2), then "the Gentile world." Wesley marks the Spirit's "twofold office — toward the world" (convicting) and "toward believers" (guiding, v.12).

The Reformed voice reads the gift's excellence. Calvin: having promised the Spirit, Christ "praises the excellence of the gift from its effect," which will not only guide and protect the disciples but "subdue the world." Lightfoot adds the historical force — the Spirit, absent some four hundred years, poured out so wonderfully would "evince to the world that Jesus was the true Messiah." Two offices are joined here: the Spirit comes not only to comfort the church but to prosecute the world — to convict it, by irrefutable proof through the apostles' preaching, of three great matters which the next verses define (v.9).

The threefold conviction — of sin, righteousness, and judgment — which the next verses define, is the Spirit's answer to a world that condemned Christ, turning the verdict back upon his accusers.

Augustine raises the obvious objection before answering it. Had Christ himself not already reproved the world on each of these counts — of sin, when he said that if he had not come and spoken to them they would have had no sin; of righteousness, when he prayed that the world had not known the righteous Father; of judgment, when he foretold the sentence on those at the left hand? The Spirit's work, then, is not a new charge but the pressing home of one already laid.

The Spirit thus turns the world's own verdict against it, prosecuting where men had presumed to sit in judgment on him (John 7:7).
9:
The first of the three convictions is stated in six words, "Of sin, because they believe not on me," and the commentators divide over whether the sin meant is unbelief itself or sin in general with unbelief at its root.

The grammatical-historical readers weigh it carefully. Ellicott: "this should not be interpreted... of the sin of unbelief, but of sin generally; unbelief in Christ is stated as the cause of sin" — sin being "the disordered action of powers that have lost their controlling principle," and Christ "the revelation of the Father." Barnes, by contrast, places the rejection of Christ first as "the sin of chief magnitude," the foremost of which men are guilty. Robertson: without this conviction men keep "a pride of intellectual superiority in refusing to believe."

The Reformed voice grounds conviction in this beginning. Calvin: "the conviction commences with the demonstration of sin; for the commencement of spiritual" life is to know our guilt. Gill applies it first to "the Jews, in disbelieving, rejecting, and crucifying Christ," the sin charged by Peter at Pentecost (Acts 2:36-37).

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke ties it to prophecy and Pentecost: the sin of "not receiving me as the Messiah, though my mission was accredited by the very miracles the prophets foretold" (Isaiah 35:5-6). Wesley: "of sin — particularly of unbelief, which is the confluence of all sins." Whether unbelief is pressed as the chief sin (Barnes, Wesley) or as the root and cause of all sin (Ellicott), the agreement is that the Spirit's first work is to break the world's complacency by convicting it of its guilt in refusing Christ — the necessary beginning before righteousness can be sought (v.10).

Only the heart convicted of sin will hunger for the righteousness the next verse reveals (v.10); conviction is the doorway to grace.

Gill fixes the primary reference before widening it. The sin chiefly meant is that of the Jews in disbelieving, rejecting and crucifying Christ, which the Spirit charged upon them through Peter at Pentecost with such evidence that, "pricked to the heart," they cried out, "what shall we do?" From there the application widens to the ordinary work of the Spirit through the preached word, convincing men of the corruption of their nature and the sin that dwells in them.

Conviction of sin, the witnesses agree, is the doorway to grace, for none seeks the righteousness of Christ who is not first humbled (v.10).
10:
The second clause follows, "Of righteousness, because I go to my Father, and ye see me no more," and most of the commentators take the righteousness to be Christ's own vindicated innocence, proved by his going to the Father.

The grammatical-historical and Wesleyan-Arminian readers fix the sense. Barnes: this "refers to the righteousness or innocence of Jesus himself" — condemned as guilty, yet the Spirit would convince the world "that he was innocent," his resurrection and ascension the proof. Clarke: "of my innocence and holiness, because I go to my Father; of which my resurrection and ascension shall be complete proofs," answering the charge that he was an impostor. Wesley: "of righteousness... but I could not go to him if I were not righteous."

Lightfoot raises the old question — "whether his personal and inherent, or his communicated and justifying righteousness" — and allows "both may be meant." Ellicott: the world is convinced of "the righteousness of Christ, not that of the world," the going to the Father being its demonstration.

The Reformed voice marks the sequence. Calvin: "we must attend to the succession of steps"; men "will never hunger and thirst for righteousness" until "moved by a conviction" of sin, after which the Spirit reveals the righteousness found in the ascended Christ. Robertson: "without Christ they lose the sense of righteousness," seen in "the new morals" of an age that has let him go. The second conviction follows: the Spirit convicts the world that the Jesus it condemned as a sinner was in truth the Righteous One — vindicated by his return to the Father — so that true righteousness is found not in the world but in him; and the third conviction follows, of judgment (v.11).

Gill sets out what the vindication had to answer. Christ had been traduced as a wicked man, called a sinner and a friend of publicans and sinners, charged with blasphemy and sedition, accused of familiarity with Satan and even of having a devil. All of this the Spirit proved slander, "by the mouth of Peter, on the day of Pentecost," to the conviction of the very people who had said it; and the outpouring itself was the demonstration, since it showed that he had reached the Father and received from him the promise he then shed abroad.
11:
The third conviction — the Spirit demonstrating that Satan is condemned and his power broken by the cross — closes the triad: "Of judgment, because the prince of this world is judged."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the reference. Robertson: "the prince of this world hath been judged" (perfect passive, "he stands condemned"), as in John 12:31 and John 14:30 — "the sinful world is in his grip, but he will be cast out." Ellicott: the perfect marks "the completion of the condemnation"; "the prince of this world hath been and remaineth judged." Barnes: the death of Christ "was a judgment or a condemnation of Satan," proving that God "will execute justice on all his foes."

The Reformed voice and Lightfoot read the victory. Lightfoot: "the prince of this world was judged when our Saviour overcame him by the obedience of his death" (Hebrews 2:14), the first instance being the resurrection, the next the loosing of the Gentiles by the gospel. Calvin: the gospel's light "manifests that the world has been brought into a state of good order by the victory of Christ, by which he overturned the authority" of Satan.

Lightfoot sets the saying against a rabbinic expectation it quietly overturns. It was held among the Jews that under the Messiah Israel would not be arraigned at all, only the nations — indeed that Israel would sit in judgment on the nations rather than come under judgment itself. But one who has already sentenced "the author of all unbelief," Lightfoot answers, will as surely sentence every unbeliever. Gill adds how the thing was publicly made out: what was disputed was Christ's own authority to judge, and the Spirit established it through Peter's preaching, the outpouring itself standing as evidence that he was raised, enthroned and declared Lord.

The Wesleyan-Arminian voices read the dethroning and its limit. Clarke: Satan's "usurped power... now to be greatly restrained, and by and by totally destroyed" (Colossians 2:15; Revelation 12:10). Wesley: "the prince of this world is judged, and in consequence dethroned... yet those who reject the deliverance offered them will remain slaves of Satan still." The third completes the triad: the Spirit convicts the world that the cross was the judgment of its prince — Satan condemned and his grip broken — so that men are without excuse if they remain under a defeated tyrant rather than coming to the victorious Christ (v.8).
12:
"I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now." The witnesses read the principle of progressive revelation — truth withheld until the disciples, taught by the Spirit, could receive it.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the meaning. Robertson: bastazein, "to bear" (Acts 15:10); "the untaught cannot get the full benefit of teaching" (1 Corinthians 3:1; Hebrews 5:11-14) — "the progressive nature of revelation is a necessity." Ellicott: the "many things" are those into which the Spirit will guide them (v.13), "parts of the revelation which the minds of the disciples are not yet fitted to receive." Lightfoot lists them — the Christian sabbath, the abolishing of the Jewish, the rejection of the nation, the calling of the Gentiles.

The Latin and Eastern fathers guard the verse from abuse. Theophylact: "all heretics, when their fables are" exposed, appeal to this — but Christ does not license new doctrines. Augustine of Hippo treats it as "a subject of needful inquiry." Hilary uses the context to fix the Spirit's procession — "sent by the Son, and proceeds from the Father."

The Reformed and Wesleyan-Arminian voices read the weakness and the supply. Calvin: their "ignorance" still kept them "in perplexity," "the weakness of the flesh" obstructing them. Wesley: "concerning my passion, death, resurrection, and the consequences" — "these things we have, not in uncertain traditions, but in the Acts, the Epistles, and the Revelation." The principle drawn out is this: revelation is progressive, fitted to the receiver's capacity; Christ withholds what they cannot yet bear, not to leave them in the dark but because the Spirit will soon lead them into the fulness of truth (v.13) — and this is no warrant for novel revelations beyond what the Spirit then gave the apostles.

Augustine guards the verse against an abuse it has long attracted. Heretics appeal to it whenever their fables are rejected for extravagance, as though these were the very things the disciples could not then bear, or as though the Spirit might teach what "even the unclean spirit is ashamed openly to teach and preach." He draws the needed distinction: bad doctrines that natural shame cannot bear are one thing, good doctrines that our poor understanding cannot bear quite another.

The fathers rightly add that this is no licence for novel revelations beyond what the Spirit then gave the apostles — the 'many things' are the apostolic deposit, not later inventions.
13:
The great promise is given here, "Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself," and in it the commentators find the charter of apostolic inspiration.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the scope. Barnes: "a full promise that they would be inspired and guided in founding the new church." Ellicott: "into all the truth" — "not that the Holy Spirit will fully guide them into truth, but that he will be their guide into the fulness of truth." Robertson notes the masculine demonstrative ekeinos for the Spirit, a mark of personality. Clarke: "he will consider your feeble infant state, and... lead and guide you" as a father a child.

The Latin father probes that last clause. Augustine of Hippo treats it as "a subject of needful inquiry" — he speaks not independently but from the Father and the Son.

He records, too, that the copies differ, some reading that he will teach them everything and others that he will lead them into it; and of the next clause, that he will show them things to come, Augustine says there is no need to linger, since it raises no question demanding exposition. Gill marks its breadth against the first occasion: the coming meant is chiefly the descent at Pentecost, yet what is said holds of that office at large and of his working upon others since.

The Reformed and Eastern voices name him the perfect Teacher. Calvin: the Spirit is "perfect Master," given "that they might deliver from hand to hand the wisdom which they had received from him." Cyril of Jerusalem: "the Father gives to the Son, and the Son shares with the Holy Ghost." The promise is of a guided fullness: the apostles are to be led into the whole truth of the gospel by one who speaks on no authority of his own but conveys what is the Father's and the Son's — the ground both of the New Testament's inspiration and of its perfect harmony with Christ, whom the Spirit comes to glorify (v.14).
14:
The Spirit's central office — not to erect a new kingdom but to glorify the Son and unfold his riches — is set out plainly: "He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the promise. Robertson: "this is the glory of the Holy Spirit, to glorify Jesus Christ"; "he shall take of mine" is "a definite promise of the Spirit's guidance in interpreting Christ," fulfilled in Peter's Pentecost sermon and in Paul. Ellicott: the future guidance of v.13 "will be the revelation of the many things of Christ himself which they cannot bear now." Barnes: the Spirit "shall receive his commission" from the Son to do his will.

The Reformed voice guards against a false notion of progress. Calvin: "the Spirit will not come to erect any new kingdom, but rather to confirm the glory given to him"; "many foolishly imagine that Christ taught only the first lessons, and then sent the disciples to a higher school" — making the gospel "of no greater value" — but the Spirit only confirms what was taught already.

The Eastern voices trace the giving from Father to Son and from Son to church. Origen reflects on "the life which is Christ"; Cyril of Jerusalem: "the Father gives to the Son, and the Son shares with the Holy Ghost." Gill: the Spirit glorifies him "in the ministration of the Gospel," asserting his full deity and ascribing to him the works and worship of God. On the Spirit’s relation to Christ there is one voice: the Spirit is no rival to him nor the herald of some teaching beyond him, but his interpreter and glorifier — taking what is his and showing it to the church, which is why all true spiritual experience centres on him, not on novelties; and what is his, the next verse explains, is the Father's own (v.15).

Origen draws a distinction that bears on the glorifying. The Saviour is some things not to himself but to others, and some things both to himself and to others; so that to be glorified by the Spirit in the church takes nothing from what he is in himself.
15:
A sweeping claim of the Son's equality with the Father, and the ground of the Spirit's whole work, stands in one sentence: "All things that the Father hath are mine: therefore said I, that he shall take of mine, and shall shew it unto you."

The grammatical-historical and Wesleyan-Arminian readers press the deity. Barnes: "no one could have said this who was not equal with the Father" (Matthew 28:18; Matthew 11:27); the union so intimate that "whatever was done in relation to the Son was also done in regard to the Father" (John 14:9). Clarke: "if Christ had not been equal to God, could he have said this without blasphemy?" — the Spirit being "the ambassador of the Son, as the Son is the ambassador of the Father." Wesley, tersely: "could any creature say this?"

The Reformed voice guards the order while affirming the equality. Calvin: lest it be thought Christ "took away from the Father what he claimed for himself, he acknowledges that he has received from the Father all that he communicates to us by the Spirit"; "he speaks in the person of the Mediator, for we must draw out of his fulness" (John 1:16). Robertson: this explains "how and why the Holy Spirit can reveal to the disciples" what they need.

Clarke supplies the figure that holds the whole arrangement together: as Christ is the Father's ambassador, so the Spirit is the ambassador of the Son, coming vested with his authority, "the interpreter and executor of his will." Gill narrows what the "all things" chiefly means here. Since Christ is speaking of what the Spirit receives from him and shows to his people, the reference is less to the bare divine nature than to the blessings of grace stored up for the chosen and the doctrines of grace, "those deep things," which it is the Spirit's peculiar work to reveal and apply.

The Eastern Cyril of Jerusalem joins it to the giving that passes from Father to Son and from Son to church. The claim is weighed and allowed: the Spirit takes "of mine" precisely because all the Father's are the Son's — a claim no creature could make, asserting Christ's full deity, yet spoken "in the person of the Mediator" so that the Father remains the fountain; the whole securing that the Spirit's revelation is nothing less than the riches of God himself shown to the church. From this height Christ returns to the nearer matter of his departure and return (v.16).
16:
"A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me, because I go to the Father." The witnesses read the riddling promise — the brief darkness of his death giving way to the joy of seeing him again.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the two intervals. Robertson: the first "little while" is "the brief period now till Christ's death" (John 7:33; John 13:33); the second, "the period between the death and the resurrection" (Friday to Sunday); "ye shall see me" of the spiritual and risen seeing (16:22). Barnes and Clarke: "hidden from view in the grave," then "I will rise and show myself to you."

The Eastern and Latin fathers read the purpose and the obscurity. Chrysostom: he "again depresses them" after comforting, "to accustom them" to bear his absence. Augustine of Hippo: the words "were so obscure to the disciples" that they puzzled over them (v.17). Lightfoot weighs whether the "seeing" is personal or virtual — "ye shall not see me personally, but virtually."

The Reformed voice reads the pastoral aim. Calvin: Christ "often forewarned the apostles of his departure, partly that they might bear it with greater courage, partly that they might desire more ardently the grace of the Spirit," of which they had little desire "so long as they had Christ present with them in body." Henry: he tells them "of the comfort he designed them." The shape of the saying is agreed: the saying folds death and resurrection into two short "little whiles" — a brief sorrow swallowed by a returning joy — but its very obscurity, owing to the disciples' grief and dullness, sets them inquiring among themselves, which Christ will graciously answer (v.19).

Chrysostom explains why the hard word is repeated rather than softened. Having lifted their spirits with the promise of the Spirit, Christ presses the departure on them again to accustom them to the mention of it, so that they may bear it well when it comes; "for nothing so quiets the troubled mind, as the continued recurrence to the subject of its grief." Bede fills in the stages the first little while covers: taken that night by the Jews, crucified the next morning, buried in the evening, and so withdrawn from all human sight.

The saying both tests and tenderly leads them, the obscurity itself driving them to the inquiry Christ longs to answer (v.19).
17:
The disciples fall to conferring among themselves over the riddle of the two "little whiles": "Then said some of his disciples among themselves, What is this that he saith unto us, A little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me: and, Because I go to the Father?"

The grammatical-historical readers fix the scene. Robertson: "some of the disciples" (ellipsis of "some" before ek, as in John 7:40); "Jesus seemed to contradict himself, for the disciples took both verbs in the same sense and were still puzzled over the going to the Father" of John 14:3 — "but they talk to one another, not to Jesus."

Gill reads their state sympathetically: "before the effusion of the Spirit on them, they were attended with a great deal of ignorance," and "what through their being overwhelmed at this time with sorrow," they could not grasp it. The very confusion illustrates v.12 — there were yet things they could not bear fills the next moment: "Then said some of his disciples among themselves, What is this that he saith unto us...?."

The failure is an understandable one: the disciples, dull with grief and lacking the Spirit not yet given, cannot penetrate the saying, and turn to one another rather than to the Lord. Their whispered perplexity is the honest measure of pre-Pentecost understanding — and it sets the stage for Christ, who reads their hearts (v.19), to answer the question they were afraid to ask. The scene quietly commends inquiry that is brought, at last, to Christ himself, and exposes the limits of a faith not yet illumined by the Spirit of truth (v.13).

The scene quietly commends inquiry that is brought, at last, to Christ himself, the only resolver of his own dark sayings (v.25).

Gill names one more hindrance besides the grief: "the national sentiments they retained about a temporal kingdom," which left them unable to take in what he said of his death, or of its nature, use and end.

Their confusion, far from being concealed, is set down by the Evangelist as the honest record of disciples not yet illumined by the Spirit of truth (v.13).
18:
The disciples' frank confession of bafflement is what the verse preserves: "They said therefore, What is this that he saith, A little while? we cannot tell what he saith."

The grammatical-historical reader fixes the moment. Robertson: "the questions to Jesus cease and the disciples frankly confess to each other their own ignorance" — "we know not what he saith." The repeated stumbling-point is the phrase "a little while" of v.16, which they cannot reconcile with his going to the Father.

Gill reads the universality of the perplexity: "one, and all of them; the inquiry became universal." None could penetrate the saying, for the Spirit who would guide them into all truth (v.13) was not yet given.

What the verse records is simply this: the verse simply records the honest helplessness of the disciples before a saying too deep for their present state — a helplessness that, far from being concealed by the Evangelist, is set down plainly. It is the very condition Christ described in v.12, that there were things they could not yet bear; and it prepares the way for him, reading their hearts, to take up their unspoken question and answer it directly (v.19), turning their confusion toward the promise of a sorrow swallowed up in joy.

The Eastern and Latin fathers put the perplexity into the disciples' own mouths. Chrysostom allows two causes at once: either sorrow had confused their minds, or the obscurity of the words themselves prevented their understanding and made them appear contradictory. He frames the deadlock as they must have felt it — "if we shall see thee, how dost thou go? if thou go, how shall we see thee?" — and so they fall back on the bare admission, "we cannot tell what he said." Augustine adds a telling comparison: when Christ had said simply that he went to the Father, without the "little while," he had seemed to speak plainly enough; it is the added measure of time that has darkened the whole. What was obscure to them before the event, he notes, is manifest to us after it.

None could penetrate the saying, for the Spirit who would guide them into all truth was not yet given, and grief had dulled their hearts (v.6); the Evangelist sets down their helplessness without disguise, that we might see how far short understanding falls before the Spirit opens the word.
19:
"Now Jesus knew that they were desirous to ask him, and said unto them..." The witnesses read Christ's reading of their unspoken hearts — a quiet proof of his deity — and his gracious anticipation of their question.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the knowledge. Robertson: "Jesus perceived" (egnō) their desire to ask, the imperfect in indirect discourse "just like our English." Ellicott: "this spirit of inquiry which he reads in their hearts" (John 2:25; John 6:6) "he proceeds to answer" — "the purpose of his enigmatic saying has been accomplished": their attention is roused.

The Reformed voice draws the deity and the lesson. Gill: "this is a proof of Christ's deity, that he is the omniscient God who knows all things, what is in man, even the secrets of the heart" — not their whisperings only but "their secret desires to ask him." Calvin: "though sometimes the Lord appears to speak to the deaf, he at length cures the ignorance of his disciples"; our duty is that "our slowness of apprehension may not be accompanied by either pride or indolence, but... humble and desirous to learn."

The Wesleyan-Arminian Wesley: Jesus spoke "preventing their question." The initiative is wholly his: Christ, knowing the heart, takes up the very question the disciples were too perplexed or timid to voice — an act both of divine omniscience and of tender condescension, meeting their bewilderment (v.18) not with rebuke but with the promise that their coming sorrow would be turned to joy (v.20).

The Eastern and Latin voices mark the mercy of the moment. Their "merciful Master, understanding their ignorance and doubts," replied so as to explain what he had said rather than leaving them to their conferring. Alcuin fills out the two spans they could not measure: the little while in which they would not see him is the three days he rested in the grave, and the little while in which they should see him the forty days of his appearing, from the passion to the ascension — and only for that little while, because he was not going to stay always in the body here, but by the humanity he had assumed to ascend to heaven.

His knowing the heart is, the Reformed voice insists, a clear proof that he is the omniscient God (John 2:25).
20:
The great reversal — the disciples' grief at the cross transformed by the resurrection — is the burden of the saying: "Verily, verily... ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the contrast. Robertson: "ye shall weep and lament" (the loud lamentations of the east), "shall rejoice" (the world) in "violent contrast" — picture "the women on the way to the Cross" (Luke 23:27). Barnes: "at my crucifixion... the world" — "wicked men," the Jews who sought his death — "will rejoice that their object was obtained," but the disciples' sorrow "shall be turned into joy" at his rising (John 20:20).

The Reformed voice reads the purpose. Calvin: he shows why he foretold his departure and "added a promise about his speedy return" — that they might understand "the aid of the Spirit was highly necessary"; "a hard and severe temptation awaits you, for when I am removed by death, the world will proclaim its triumph."

Barnes presses the application further than the disciples could then see. Their greatest apparent calamity would prove, in the end, the source of their highest comfort: the death now grieving them would procure peace and pardon in this life and eternal joy in the world to come. From this he draws a rule for every affliction — "if we could see the whole case, we should rejoice" — and a word on the apparent triumphs of the wicked, which may breed present grief in Christians yet are overruled for good: their joy turned into mourning and the mourning of Christians into joy, while the very deed they do is made to serve "the glory of God and the good of his people" (Psalms 76:10). Clarke adds a note on the word: in several parts of this discourse "the world" means the unbelieving and rebellious among the Jews, the chief priests and scribes and Pharisees who would triumph as though their bad cause were crowned with success.

The Eastern Cyril of Jerusalem joins the witness to eternal life. The contrast is the whole point: the verse sets the brief, bitter sorrow of the cross — when the world gloats and the disciples weep — against the lasting joy of the resurrection that will swallow it up; the same reversal the next verse illustrates by the woman in travail, whose anguish is forgotten in the joy of birth (v.21). The grief is real but momentary; the joy, real and abiding.
21:
The homely illustration of sorrow swallowed in joy carries the whole figure: "A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow... but as soon as she is delivered... she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the figure. Robertson: "the woman," any woman; "whenever she is about to bear," a "common Old Testament image for pain." Ellicott multiplies the prophetic parallels (Isaiah 26:17-18; Isaiah 66:7-8; Jeremiah 4:31; Hosea 13:13). Clarke notes "a man is born" stands for "a human creature."

The Reformed voice draws the comparison out. Calvin: the figure confirms that not only will sorrow be followed by joy, "but also that it contains in itself the ground and occasion of" the joy — as a mother, the grief once past, gives herself wholly to gladness. Gill: "as it is with a woman in travail, so it was now with them."

Two further touches are worth keeping. Robertson notes the force of "her hour is come" — the hour of birth, which a woman "knows is like a living death" — and that the word for anguish is thlipsis, the usual term for tribulation. Ellicott puts the whole figure in a sentence: the thought is of the joy of maternity swallowing up the pangs of childbirth; "these cease to exist, but that continues," and "she forgets the one in the fulness of the other." He gathers the prophets more widely still (Isaiah 21:3; Jeremiah 22:23; Micah 4:9-10). Calvin adds the qualification that gives the comparison its edge: the issue of all griefs "cannot be otherwise than unfavorable, unless when they are blessed in Christ," but the cross of Christ "always contains in itself the victory."

The figure teaches more than sequence: the travail-image teaches that the disciples' anguish at the cross is not merely followed by joy but is its very birth-pang — the suffering itself bringing forth the gladness of the resurrection. The pain is sharp but purposeful and brief; the joy, once the new life is born, so fills the heart that the anguish is "remembered no more." The next verse applies the figure directly: their present sorrow will give way to a joy no man can take from them (v.22).
22:
"And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you." The witnesses read the application — a present grief, a promised reunion, and an unassailable joy.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the promise. Barnes: "after my resurrection"; the joy so grounded in the certainty of his rising that "neither threats nor persecutions... shall ever take it away" — "this prediction was remarkably fulfilled." Robertson: the metaphor "points to the resurrection of Jesus which did change the grief of the disciples to gladness." Clarke notes some read "shall take away" (future), the resurrection "so completely demonstrated... that their joy should be great and permanent."

The Reformed voice reads the perpetuity. Calvin: "the value of joy is greatly enhanced by its perpetuity"; the world's joy, sought "only in fading things," is soon lost, but this joy is secure, drawn from the risen Christ.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Wesley guards against misuse: this "gives us no authority to assert all believers must come into a state of darkness; they never need lose their peace, or love, or the witness that they are children of God" — losing it only "through sin, or ignorance, or vehement temptation, or bodily disorder." The promise is measured and absolute at once: the disciples' present sorrow is real but temporary, to be turned at the resurrection into a joy so anchored in the living Christ that no enemy can wrest it away — the abiding gladness of those who have seen the Lord, and the firstfruits of the access in prayer the next verses unfold (v.23).

Gill draws the application past the apostles to any believer left without the sight of Christ. Sin, Satan and the hard dispensations of providence all bring their sorrows, yet none touches a believer so nearly as absence from him, and for reason: he is "so nearly related to them, being their everlasting Father, kind husband, loving brother, and faithful friend," and there is none like him in their esteem in heaven or earth. He is "the very life of their souls"; his gracious presence is life and his absence as death, so that they cannot be at ease but are restless and inquiring after him until he returns, which he does in his own time.

It is the firstfruits of the new access in prayer that the following verses unfold, joy and asking bound together (v.24).
23:
The new era of prayer — direct access to the Father in the name of the Son — opens here: "And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily... Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the double sense of "ask." Robertson: the first "ask" may mean "question" (no need to inquire, as in verses 19, 30, the Spirit now illumining them) or "request," the second clearly "request" in the Father's name. Ellicott takes "ask me nothing" of the Paraclete's full illumination, so that they "shall not need to ask the meaning" as before (Acts 1:6). Barnes sees both senses — they had depended on Christ present, now they will ask the Father.

The Eastern and Latin fathers read the day of the resurrection. Chrysostom: "in that day," when risen, "ye shall ask me nothing" — no longer "Show us the Father" (John 14:8). Augustine of Hippo treats the asking "in my name" as the great theme. The Puritan Henry distinguishes "asking by way of enquiry, the asking of the ignorant," from "asking by way of request."

Chrysostom turns the promise into a comfort against the absence itself. They are not to think that because he will no longer be with them they are therefore forsaken: "my name will be a still greater protection to you than my presence." The point is pressed to its edge — that he who is neither seen nor petitioned, but only named before the Father, will do miracles.

The Reformed and Wesleyan-Arminian voices read the new light and the open hand. Calvin: a "grace of the Spirit" by which they receive "so great light of understanding as would raise them to heavenly mysteries." Wesley: "ye shall not question me about anything... for you will know all things clearly," and "whatsoever ye shall ask, he will give it — our Lord here gives us a charte blanche." Two gifts belong to that day: in the age of the Spirit the disciples will both need fewer questions, being inwardly taught, and enjoy a new boldness — asking the Father directly in Christ's name, with the promise that he will give; a gift the next verse urges them to begin to use (v.24).
24:
An invitation to a new kind of prayer is pressed upon them, with its end named in the same breath: "Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the "hitherto." Robertson: "up till now the disciples had not used Christ's name in prayer to the Father, but after the resurrection they are to do so" — "a distinct plea for parity with the Father and for worship like the Father." Barnes: "this great truth — that we must approach God" through Christ — had not yet been their practice. Ellicott ties the fulness of joy to v.22.

The Reformed voice and Lightfoot read the Mediator. Calvin: the fathers "were not accustomed to pray without a Mediator," trained by the high priest entering the holy place and the sacrifices; now that Mediator is openly Christ. Lightfoot refers the "nothing in my name" to "the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit" — they had asked nothing extraordinary in the name of Jesus the Messiah until now.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke: "ask in my name, and ye shall receive all the salvation ye thus request, the consequence of which shall be that your joy shall be full." A door is set open here: a new privilege of prayer opens — to ask the Father expressly in the name of the Son — and its purpose is not bare supply but the completion of the disciples' joy, the very joy promised at the resurrection (v.22). Prayer in Christ's name, the chapter teaches, is the appointed channel by which the believer's gladness is filled to the full.

Barnes marks the timing as deliberate. That we must approach God through a Mediator was "reserved for the last" of all Christ taught them, held back to the close of his ministry, when they were in some degree prepared for it; and amid coming trials and wants, and a sense of their own weakness and unworthiness, they would find how precious the privilege was. Though he would be bodily absent, their blessings would still come through "the same unchanging Friend." Lightfoot, having cleared the difficulty, declines to go further: what here "might give occasion for scholastical discussion" he leaves wholly to the schools.

The Mediator thus opens the way the fathers approached only in shadow, that the believer's joy may be full (v.23).
25:
The promise of fuller, clearer teaching after the resurrection and Pentecost is the subject of this word: "These things have I spoken unto you in proverbs: but the time cometh, when I shall no more speak unto you in proverbs, but I shall shew you plainly of the Father."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the words. Robertson: "in proverbs" (paroimiais, John 10:6); "shall tell" (apangelō) "plainly" (parrēsia, John 7:13). Ellicott: "in parables," referring specially to what he said from v.16; "the hour would come when he would speak no more in parables, but tell them plainly of the Father." Clarke fixes "the time" as "the interval from his resurrection to his ascension," the forty days of instruction (Acts 1:3).

The Reformed voice reads the encouragement. Calvin: the intention is "to give courage to his disciples, that, entertaining good hopes of making better progress, they may not think the instruction useless," nor suppose "that Christ did not wish to be understood." Gill lists the things spoken obscurely — the Father, the mansions, the way, communion, the manifestation.

Both Gill and the Wesleyan readers fill out what had been spoken darkly. Gill lists it: the Father and his house with its many mansions, the preparing of a place and the way to it, the communion to be manifested to them and not to the world, the vine and its branches, the departure and the return, the sorrow and the joy figured in the woman in travail. All of it, he says, "one would think, were plain and easy to be understood," yet in their present state it seemed so many dark sayings. Clarke defines the manner: words which, besides their plain literal sense, carry another, heavenly things represented "through the medium of earthly"; and he dates the promised plainness to the forty days between the resurrection and the ascension. Barnes presses the cause of the dullness — minds "filled with Jewish prejudices, and unwilling to believe that he was about to die," to which the plainest declaration would seem involved in mystery.

The veil is temporary: Christ's present teaching, veiled in figure and met by the disciples' dullness, is not his last word; the day of the Spirit will bring a plain and open showing of the Father — fulfilled in the risen Lord's instruction and supremely in the Spirit's illumination (v.13). The obscurity is temporary; the promised clarity, the inheritance of the Spirit-taught church.
26:
"At that day ye shall ask in my name: and I say not unto you, that I will pray the Father for you." The witnesses read a saying that, far from denying Christ's intercession, magnifies the Father's own love for believers.

The grammatical-historical readers guard against misreading. Robertson: "Christ did pray for the disciples" (John 14:16; 17:9) "and he prays also for sinners" (Luke 23:34; 1 John 2:1); here the point is "the special love of God for disciples of Jesus" (John 14:23). Barnes: elsewhere "Jesus ever liveth to make intercession" (Hebrews 7:25), so this means not that he will not pray, but that the Father needs no persuading.

The Reformed voice resolves the apparent contradiction. Calvin: there "appears to be a contradiction," but the meaning is that whatever they need, "God will refuse nothing that shall be asked of his Son" — the Father's readiness is such that Christ need not be represented as wringing favours from a reluctant God.

Barnes guards the saying from the obvious misreading. Christ had already promised to pray the Father and to send the Comforter (John 14:16), was about to offer the prayer of the next chapter for them, and is represented throughout the New Testament as ever living to make intercession (Hebrews 7:25; Hebrews 9:24). The declaration therefore does not mean that he would not intercede, only that there was then no need to mention it again; what they needed telling was that God was ready and willing to confer on them every needful blessing. Gill adds what changed at Pentecost: they were blessed with the Spirit as a spirit of grace and supplication, understood the throne of grace better, and found greater assistance at it.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke and Wesley read the Father's free love. Clarke: "I need not tell you that I will continue your intercessor... besides, the Father himself needs no entreaty, for he loves you." Wesley: "this in nowise implies that he will not" pray; "the Father himself now loves you... because of the faith and love which he hath wrought in you." What matters is where the eyes are directed: the verse does not set aside Christ's priestly intercession but lifts the disciples' eyes to the Father's own delight in them — they come in the Son's name to a Father who already loves them, so that prayer is not the storming of a closed heart but the asking of an open one (v.27).
27:
The ground of the Father's love — the disciples' love for Christ and faith in his divine origin — is given as the reason: "For the Father himself loveth you, because ye have loved me, and have believed that I came out from God."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the words. Robertson: "loveth" (philei) "the word for warm and friendly love," used here of God's love for the disciples, where John 3:16 uses agapaō for his love for the world; "ye have loved me" (perfect, "loved and still love me warmly") "and have believed." Barnes and Ellicott refer it to John 14:21 and 14:23 — the communion between the Father and the heart that receives his love.

The Reformed voice reads the bond. Calvin: "the only bond of our union with God is to be united to Christ; and we are united to him by a faith which is not feigned, but which springs from sincere affection." Gill: the Father "loved them as well, and as much as the Son did, and of himself too," from everlasting, proved in giving his Son and in calling them by grace.

Calvin presses an objection most readers feel and few voice. If God begins to love us only when we have loved Christ, then "the commencement of salvation is from ourselves, because we have anticipated the grace of God" — against which he sets the whole tenor of Scripture, which has God choosing the unlovely and making a new heart where there was none (1 John 4:19; Ezekiel 36:26; Romans 10:20). His answer distinguishes two moments. God loves his own secretly before they are called, indeed before they are created; but until they are reconciled they are justly reckoned enemies, as Paul has it, "when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son" (Romans 5:10). Only then are they said to be loved, when they hold the pledge of a fatherly kindness in the God they once shrank from as an offended judge. Ellicott notices the order of the clauses, belief placed after affection, and reads in it a hint that their convictions came of hearts first opened; he adds that several of the better manuscripts end the verse "that I came forth from the Father."

Boldness is given a ground: the warrant for the believer's bold approach (v.26) is the Father's own warm affection — kindled toward those who love the Son and believe he came from God. The love is not earned but answered: God loves those who, by his grace, love and trust his Son. Faith in Christ's divine origin and love for his person are thus the marks of those whom the Father himself cherishes — the very ones Christ came forth from the Father to seek (v.28).
28:
"I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world: again, I leave the world, and go to the Father." The witnesses read this as a fourfold summary of the whole gospel — and a fresh assertion of Christ's deity.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke gives the famous outline: "I came forth from the Father — with whom I existed from eternity in glory; am come into the world — by my incarnation; I leave the world — by my death; and go to the Father — by my ascension. These four words contain the whole economy of the gospel" and "a consummate abridgment of the Christian faith."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the terms. Robertson: "I came out from the Father" (aorist, "the Incarnation"), "am come" (perfect, "the Incarnation is now a permanent" fact). Barnes and Ellicott: he repeats with emphasis what the disciples now believe (v.27) — "heaven, and not earth, is my home," and he returns to the Father.

The Reformed voice reads the deity. Calvin: "this mode of expression draws our attention to the divine power which is in Christ"; faith "would not be steady, if it did not perceive his divine power; for his death and resurrection, the two pillars of faith, would be of little avail if heavenly power were not connected with them." Henry: he comforts them that "though he was leaving the world, he was returning to his Father." All four dwell on its compass: one sentence traces the whole course, a creed in miniature that grounds faith in his divine origin and destiny, and it is this summary that draws from the disciples their glad confession (v.29).

Gill is careful to say what the coming forth does not mean. Not the eternal filiation, nor a coming forth in grace in the counsel and covenant of peace, nor an appointment as Mediator from everlasting, but the coming in the flesh in the fulness of time — which supposes that he existed as a divine person before, and was with the Father, and came with his knowledge and will, sent and yet willing, not forced. Nor does it suppose local motion or change of place, since he fills heaven and earth with his presence, but only the taking of our nature into unity with that person; nor any separation from the Father, in whose bosom he lay when he was made flesh.
29:
The disciples' glad response — they feel the light breaking, and welcome the plain word — breaks out at once: "His disciples said unto him, Lo, now speakest thou plainly, and speakest no proverb."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the moment. Robertson: "no wayside saying, no dark saying" (John 10:6; v.25). Ellicott: "the emphasis is upon the word now" — Christ had said the hour would come when he would speak plainly (v.25), and "his last words have explained what they before could not" grasp. Barnes: their perplexity over v.16 is now resolved by v.28, "and they expressed themselves satisfied."

The Eastern and Latin fathers read their state. Chrysostom: "the disciples were so refreshed with the thought of being in favour with the Father, that they say they are sure he knows all things." Augustine of Hippo reflects on "the inward state of Christ's disciples" — children spoken to of great things in a way fitted to children.

The Reformed voice tempers their confidence. Calvin: "this shows how great was the efficacy of that consolation, for it suddenly brought into cheerfulness minds formerly broken"; yet "it is certain they did not yet understand fully the meaning of Christ's discourse" — "the mere odour of it refreshed them." The confession is welcomed and weighed: the disciples, cheered by the plain word about the Father, gladly declare their understanding — a real but immature faith, kindled more by relief than by full comprehension, which the next verse will voice as a confident creed (v.30), and which Christ will gently test (v.31).

The Eastern and Latin fathers are less impressed than the disciples are with themselves. Augustine puts a sharp question: why say the hour of plain speech has come, when it was still future and only promised? Because his words continued to be dark sayings to them, and they were "so far from understanding them, that they do not even understand their not understanding them." Chrysostom marks the self-regard in it. After so many and such great things, to say only now that they were sure — and to say it "as if they were conferring a favour."

Calvin's caution holds — 'the mere odour' of the consolation refreshed them — and their confidence, voiced as a creed in the next verse (v.30), will be gently tested before the trial that scatters them.
30:
The disciples' confession — drawn from Christ's reading of their unspoken hearts — is the substance of their reply: "Now are we sure that thou knowest all things... by this we believe that thou camest forth from God."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the ground of the confession. Robertson: they had failed to understand his plain words about going to the Father (v.5), "but Jesus read their very thoughts" (v.19), "and this fact seemed to open their minds." Barnes: their difficulty over v.16 they had discussed among themselves without telling him (John 16:17-19), so when he answered the unspoken question they were convinced of his omniscience. Ellicott: they see in his knowledge of their thoughts "the fulfilment of the promise" of v.23.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Wesley reads the echo: "thou knowest all things — even our hearts... by this we believe that thou camest forth from God," echoing back Christ's own words of v.27, "implying, We believe in God; we believe also in thee." Clarke: they own him "that God who searchest the heart."

Barnes sets out the inference step by step, and it is tighter than it looks. They had not mentioned their difficulty to Christ at all, nor had he overheard their conferring; yet when his answer met the very doubt they had kept among themselves, and met it unasked, they were satisfied that he knew the heart and had assuredly come from God. Hence their further word, that there was no need for any man to ask him or lay his difficulties before him, since he knew them all already and could answer them. Gill marks the same mercy from the other side: knowing what they wished to ask, Christ prevented the question and opened a discourse that explained what they wanted to know before they could put it.

The reasoning is sound as far as it goes: the disciples ground their faith in Christ's divine origin upon his omniscience — his knowing their hearts before they spoke. It is a true confession, rightly reasoned, that his searching of the heart proves him come from God; yet, as the next verse will show, it is a confidence riper in word than in the strength to stand, which Christ must lovingly probe before the trial that will scatter them (v.31).
31:
"Jesus answered them, Do ye now believe?" The witnesses read Christ's searching reply — neither denying their faith nor flattering it, but warning of the trial to come.

The grammatical-historical readers weigh whether it is question or statement. Ellicott: "the words do not necessarily ask a question," and a sense "more in harmony with the context" takes them as an assertion — "our Lord did not doubt their present faith" (John 17:8), "but he knew" what was coming. Robertson: "their belief in Christ was genuine, but perils await them of which they are ignorant. They are too self-confident as their despair at Christ's death shows." Barnes: the question was "to put them on a full examination of their hearts."

The Reformed voice reads the gentle correction. Calvin: "as the disciples were too highly pleased with themselves, Christ reminds them that, remembering their weakness, they ought rather to confine themselves within their own little capacity"; "we never are fully aware of... our great distance from the fulness of faith, till we come to some serious trial." Gill: not a denial of their faith but "a reproof... for their security, vain confidence and boasting."

Faith is neither crushed nor flattered: the disciples' faith is real but overconfident, untested by the cross; Christ neither crushes nor inflates it, but searches it — for genuine faith, on every reading, does not yet know its own weakness until trial reveals it. The warning prepares them for the scattering he immediately foretells (v.32).

Gill weighs the tone of the question carefully. It is not that Christ calls their faith in question, nor denies they had any, nor despises it for its smallness; the reproof falls rather on "their security, vain confidence and boasting," as though their faith were so strong it could never be moved — and perhaps on the lateness of it too, that they believed no sooner and were not better established, when he had been so long with them and they had seen so many of his works. The clause can be read as a statement, "ye do believe now," and the Syriac and Arabic make it an imperative, "believe ye now." Either way it was not too late, and they would do well to go on believing. Barnes takes the question as set to put them on a full examination of their hearts, which is where the strong in faith have most need to look.

The warning is an act of love, preparing them for the scattering he immediately foretells, that they may not despair when their confidence fails (v.32).
32:
Desertion and unbroken communion are set side by side without flinching: "Behold, the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me."

The grammatical-historical readers fix the scene. Robertson: "yea, is come" (perfect), "the long-looked-for hour is so close that it has virtually begun" (John 17:1); the arrest is near. Barnes: "ye shall be scattered" (Matthew 26:31), "every man to his own home," supposing his work defeated. Clarke: "your faith will be then so shaken that ye shall run away, each striving to save himself."

The Reformed voice reads the undiminished dignity. Calvin: "this correction is added, to inform us that, when Christ is forsaken by men, he loses nothing of his dignity"; "his truth and glory are founded on himself," so that "if he is forsaken by the whole world, still he is in no degree impaired, because he is God." Gill notes the nearness — "within an hour."

Barnes fills in what the scattering came to. "Every man to his own" means to his own home: they would see him die, suppose his work defeated, and go back to their dwellings — the two on the Emmaus road probably among them — and after his death the company withdrew into Galilee and took up its old employment of fishing (John 21:1-14). To be left alone was to be left "to die without human sympathy or compassion." Against that he sets the last clause. Christ had all along trusted God, and even when the suffering wrung from him the cry of forsakenness, the words were still addressed to him as his God, "my God, my God"; and the same confidence could commit his spirit into those hands at the end (Luke 23:46).

The foretelling is exact and merciful at once: Christ foretells, with sorrowful precision, that the very disciples who just confessed him will scatter and abandon him in his hour — yet adds the great consolation that he is never truly alone, for the Father is with him. The desertion of men cannot break his communion with God; and in this he is both their warning, that self-confident faith fails under trial (v.31), and their model, that the soul kept in the Father is not alone though all forsake it. From this he turns to his closing word of peace (v.33).
33:
"These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world." The witnesses read the grand conclusion of the upper-room discourse — peace in Christ amid tribulation, grounded in his victory.

The grammatical-historical readers fix the threefold close. Robertson: "that ye may keep on having peace in me" (John 14:27), "peace to be found nowhere save in me"; "be of good cheer" (tharseite), "courage in the face of danger"; "I have overcome the world" — the perfect of settled victory. Barnes: "in me — in my presence and the aid of the Holy Spirit"; the victory is won by vanquishing "the prince of this world" (John 12:31).

The Reformed voice reads the necessity and the comfort. Calvin: he proves how needful the consolations were, since "numerous distresses await them in the world"; "all believers ought to be convinced that their life is exposed to many afflictions, that they may be disposed to exercise patience." Gill takes "these things" of the whole discourse — his departure, the mansions, union with him, the persecutions.

Gill adds what stands nearest at hand in that catalogue: the forsaking just foretold, which was itself a prelude of what the world would deal them, and over against it the Father's presence with Christ, which they might also expect to be theirs. Barnes unfolds how the victory is made theirs: by his death he brought down aid and strength from above, procuring the friendship of God and the influence of the Spirit, and by his own teaching and example, and by opening their eyes to the excellence of heavenly things, he furnished them with the means of overcoming every enemy in their turn.

The Wesleyan-Arminian Clarke reads the gift: "the peace of God is ever to be understood as including all possible blessedness — light, strength, comfort, support, a sense of the divine favour." With that the discourse closes: Christ does not promise his own escape from tribulation but peace in him through it, and the courage that flows from his finished conquest of the world. The believer's calm rests not on calm circumstances but on a Saviour who has already overcome — the note of triumph on which Jesus turns from teaching to prayer (John 17:1).
